That reads as a setup for a British-keeps-it-because-it-was-always-strategic story. The only source named is Sayer (British, 1862) and the Gibraltar National Museum, so the evidence looks one-sided. 'Told from both sides' records' is only a promise, and nothing on screen backs it up.
X.moment_you_would_leave_or_doubt: The title card with Sayer 1862 and the Gibraltar National Museum as the only sources, followed straight away by 'Only five changed who ruled it'. That sounds like the argument that Spain's attempts mostly failed. I would close the video at that point.

Y.why: It is neutral and factual. 'Historians on both sides' and a Spanish source (García Sanz 2022) next to the British ones is the signal I look for. It has no 'edge of Spain' wording and no hint of Spain as the villain. It's a little dry, and 'told from both sides' records' could still be empty.
Y.moment_you_would_leave_or_doubt: The rewind to 1704 with map labels. If the narration then says 'the British captured it' without saying Spain lost it in the War of the Spanish Succession, or if the Spanish side only appears as the attacker, I would doubt it. I would also doubt it if the Spanish source is named and then never used.

Z.why: It puts a Spanish historian (Montero, 1860, in Spanish) first and a British one second, using the same phrase. That shows both sides really are given equal footing, and it is the strongest hook. It does not take a side in the first 30 seconds. The Spanish quote is on screen in the original language, which suggests the makers did their research.
Z.moment_you_would_leave_or_doubt: Any point where the later sections use only the British sources or call Spanish attempts 'failed assaults' in a tone that mocks them. I would also doubt it if the quote is shown and then the video switches to the British story with no Spanish record.

one_change_to_the_best_version: Put the Spanish-language quote on screen for slightly longer and say the date and author out loud, and add a Spanish source name to the title card (Montero 1860 next to Sayer 1862). That way the 'both sides' claim is shown rather than just stated.
